💡 Key Takeaways
  • Battlefield 6’s first season has entered its second phase.
  • The enhancement, of course, also adds fresh content to the game in the form of the map Eastwood, as well as new hardware and fresh features for the multiplayer sandbox.
  • Industry observers note that we’ve known about the fresh content side of today’s patch for quite some time.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Battlefield 6’s first season has entered its second phase. The game received a major update earlier today, version 1.1.2.0, which delivers a host of changes to the game, many of which have been expected.

The enhancement, of course, also adds fresh content to the game in the form of the map Eastwood, as well as new hardware and fresh features for the multiplayer sandbox.

Industry observers note that we’ve known about the fresh content side of today’s patch for quite some time. The enhancement kicks off the California Resistance stage of Season 1, which is the second of three. The new Eastwood map takes place in California, and it’s a map cut from the larger Battlefield Redsec battle royale map of Fort Lyndon.

There’s a fresh limited-time mode called Sabotage - a tactical, 8v8 mode where two teams attempt to destroy as many bomb sites as possible. The other substantial new feature that arrives today is Battle Pickups.

These are powerful weapons which can be found in specific game modes (and in Portal), scattered around the map for players to pick up and use. They have limited ammo that cannot be replenished, and deliver incredible firepower.

Sources indicate that redsec players have a latest Gauntlet mission to look forward to that joins the existing modes. It’s called Rodeo and it involves a lot of vehicular action. Finally, everyone gets to unlock two new weapons: the the DB-12 shotgun, and the M327 Trait revolver sidearm. There’s also a new angled grip attachment.

The fixes and tweaks side of the patch is arguably the more interesting. Controller aim assist has received a big overhaul that essentially resets everything to open beta settings. The goal is to make infantry targeting more consistent.

It has been revealed that controller players actually get the bulk of the changes in this upgrade, which also improves input latency and stick response. Several concerns that reset aim assist values, or make it behave erratically, have been addressed.

The conversation around weapon bloom/spread doesn’t look like it’s ever going to end, because Battlefield Studios is yet again tuning gunplay to fix unintended dispersion behaviour, and decrease its intensity across the board.

Certain Challenges have had their description rewritten so their requirements can be better understood. Beyond that, you can expect several deployables to behave much more consistently, including several bug fixes there, too.

Head to the official blog for the full rundown of patch 1.1.2.0.

Eagles are eating human-sized baboons in the Sahara desert

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (573 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Popsci

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, an isolated  group of primates calls the rugged, sandstone Ennedi plateau in northern Chad, home.
  • Sources indicate that fresh research published today in the American Journal of Biological Anthropology details how these eagles appear to be preying upon these nearly human-sized baboons.
  • Our ancestors were vulnerable to several predators, including crocodiles, significant cats, and even eagles.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, an isolated  group of primates calls the rugged, sandstone Ennedi plateau in northern Chad, home. In this region in the middle of the Sahara Desert about the size of Switzerland, the olive baboons (Papio anubis) have lived a separate life away from other primate species. At 40 to 60 pounds, some olive baboons are about the size of our early hominin ancestors. But their size does not keep them safe from hungry Verreaux’s eagles (Aquila verreauxii).

Sources indicate that fresh research published today in the American Journal of Biological Anthropology details how these eagles appear to be preying upon these nearly human-sized baboons. The discovery is reshaping how scientists think about predator-prey interactions during human evolution.

Our ancestors were vulnerable to several predators, including crocodiles, significant cats, and even eagles. However, scientists believed that our species (Homo sapiens) and our hominin ancestors have been escaping these predators for roughly the past 2.5 million years. No primate over 28.6 pounds (13 kilograms) has been confirmed to be killed by raptors, so our body sizes appeared to be too heavy for even the large eagles with a 71- to 86-inch-long wingspan to pick up.

Sources indicate that in this study, the team describes skulls and bones of adult male olive baboons that bear the signature marks of eagle predation. There were talon punctures to the skulls, and various scrapes and “rakes” on the shoulder bones.

Industry observers note that “We saw the eagles while we were searching for the baboons, but we never imagined that they might be a threat to them,” Catherine Hobaiter, a study co-author and primatologist at the University of St. Andrews in Scotland, mentioned in a statement. “Then we found the first skull with a puncture mark, and then another, and another.”.

With these remains, the team was able to calculate how much the deceased baboons weighed. One individual was over 57.3 pounds (26 kilograms), well within the range of a hominin species.

Industry observers note that “Having worked in this region for about three years, I had the opportunity to visit these gueltas (pockets of water that form within rock formations) and often observed Verreaux’s eagles. I had never imagined that these predators would target primates of this size until the research team stumbled upon evidence,” added Dr. Jean Didier Akpona from the African Parks Network. “This discovery leads us to explore further the mystery that surrounds the gueltas of the Sahara Desert.”.

To defend against eagles, our primate ancestors would “mob” or charge the attacker to try to drive them away. The modern primates living in places with eagle predators often move in large groups mixed with other primate species. This also mirrors the evolutionary history of our early ancestors, who lived alongside other hominin species and other primates. While some conflict arose, plenty of cooperative advantages to sticking together also happened—like mobbing eagles.

The team hopes to learn more about the lives of the Ennedi baboons to see what other evolutionary secrets they may be holding.

“Baboons are some of the best studied monkeys in Africa, but our very first observations from Ennedi upended all sorts of notions about what these baboons should be doing—from their diet to their social lives, I can’t wait to see what latest ‘rules’ they’ll break next!” Hobaiter concluded.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

As no-drip, low-noise job sites become more the global rule rather than the exception, Volvo’s incredibly versatile EWR150 Electric wheeled excavators are proving to be a smart addition to construction and municipal fleets – that’s proving true in Luxembourg, as well.

Recent findings suggest that the Volvo EWR150 Electric wheeled excavator is helping the postage stamp nation of Luxembourg connect natural freshwater springs to a planned water reservoir, but the work has to be done in an existing groundwater protection zone, where even the smallest fuel spills or oil leaks could have serious consequences. An ideal opportunity, in other words, for a battery electric machine like the EWR150 Electric to shine.

“Sometimes I miss the sound of the engine,” says Thomas Weber, an operator on the project who’d previously worked with the conventional EWR150 wheeled excavator. “But the quieter operation of the EWR150 Electric is more beneficial for me, personally. Compared to the diesel equivalent, I find the performance and power to be identical.”.

Volvo CE took to LinkedIn to share the work being done by the Luxemburgers at construction firm Elenz, touting the Volvo’s clean, quiet running in this highly environment.

Sources indicate that for their part, Elenz executives are equally excited about the upcoming machine. “Going electric is not a regulation, but a requirement for this particular job,” explains Christoph Schommer, Managing Director of Elenz. “We are thoroughly impressed by the EWR150 Electric. Its low noise level is a major advantage here. At the same time, the machine offers plenty of power and consistently delivers the same level of energy.”.

Recent findings suggest that the EWR150 Electric is built around a 270 kWh, 600V li-ion battery pack powering an electric drive motor that’s backed by a KERS-style hydraulic boom energy-recovery system that works like regenerative braking to extend the machine’s operating time. A 0.67 m³ (~0.9 yd³) bucket with 108.5-kN (~ 24,390 lb.) breakout force is standard, and offers a, 8.95 meter (~29 foot) maximum digging reach and 5.23 meter (~17 foot) digging depth. Volvo says the machine can typically operate for 8–10 hours depending on the application.

According to recent reports, elenz is charging their EWR150 Electric overnight using a 32A L2 connection at a nearby sewage treatment plant, which also serves as the project office and a secure parking location for site equipment. By charging overnight, when Elenz’ crew isn’t working, the company has been able to integrate the massive BEV without changing their existing work schedules.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • A quartet of medical organizations has published a comprehensive set of reports calling for a coordinated plan of action to improve heart healthcare for women throughout their lifetimes.
  • The reports detail how cardiovascular health issues can be prevented, monitored, and treated from the early years of menstruation to peak fertility age to pregnancy to perimenopause to postmenopause stages.
  • The report authors call for healthcare professionals to identify heart health risks early in girls and women and to coordinate care across medical specialties.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A quartet of medical organizations has published a comprehensive set of reports calling for a coordinated plan of action to improve heart healthcare for women throughout their lifetimes.

The reports detail how cardiovascular health issues can be prevented, monitored, and treated from the early years of menstruation to peak fertility age to pregnancy to perimenopause to postmenopause stages.

The report authors call for healthcare professionals to identify heart health risks early in girls and women and to coordinate care across medical specialties.

In a recent development, they stress that females have specific biological factors that increase their risks of cardiovascular disease. Those components include hormonal and emotional factors.

In a recent development, the authors note that heart disease is the number one cause of death for females in the United States, as well as the number one cause of death during pregnancy. Yet, only 44% of females are fully aware of the dangers they face from heart disease.

The organizations issuing the reports are the American Heart Association (AHA), the American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP), the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists (ACOG), and the Society for Maternal-Fetal Medicine.

The groups presented their findings in a trio of reports published in the AHA’s flagship journal, Circulation on October 26.

“Women experience their healthcare across clinical specialties, but it often is fragmented or disconnected,” remarked Sadiya Khan, MD, the chair of the collaborative writing group for the reports and a professor of cardiovascular epidemiology at Northwestern University Feinberg School of Medicine in Chicago, in a news release.

“Specifically, these reports connect the dots for clinicians, for patients, and across health domains so that care is holistic and begins in adolescence, recognizing that women’s heart health is uniquely shaped by biological transitions not experienced by men — periods, pregnancy, perimenopause, and menopause.”.

Experts not involved in the reports told Healthline the updates were a long time coming.

Nicole Weinberg, MD, a cardiologist at Pacific Heart Institute’s Women’s Heart Center in Santa Monica, California, mentioned the reports present a positive framework for women’s health.

“Women have unique cardiovascular risk factors related to pregnancy and menopause, and certain traditional risk factors, including diabetes, may increase their risk of heart disease more significantly than they do in men,” noted Nissi Suppogu, MD, a cardiologist and medical director of the Women’s Heart Center at MemorialCare Heart & Vascular Institute at Long Beach Medical Center in California.

“Recognizing these differences is essential to identifying women at risk earlier, improving prevention strategies and ensuring they receive appropriate treatment,” she remarked.

“I am incredibly excited to see these latest reports on women’s heart health,” added Svati Shah, MD, the president-elect of the AHA, as well as the associate dean of Translational Research and the director of Precision Genomics Collaboratory in the Duke School of Medicine in North Carolina.

“They are a call to action for increasing education, research, and coordinated clinical care for women’s heart health,” Shah noted.

The organizations spelled out their recommendations in three reports.

The first report is a presidential advisory that lays out a “female-specific life course approach to the prevention and management of cardiovascular disease.”.

In it, the authors state that “girls and women uniquely experience fragmented care” across medical fields, including pediatrics, obstetrics, and gynecology.

The authors call for a “unified life course approach that addresses the female-specific interconnectedness of hormonal, psychosocial, and cardiovascular health.”.

This report breaks down the life cycle for girls and women into five stages.

“Emerging data suggest that unique biologic transitions or life stages experienced by girls and women are linked with changes in [cardiovascular disease] risk, which may be due in part to physiologic changes in sex hormones,” the authors wrote.

Weinberg remarked this life-stage breakdown is key, especially for risk reduction.

She said problems with menstruation during the teen years may be a harbinger of heart health problems later in life. The same is true for health issues during pregnancy, especially high blood pressure or high blood sugar levels.

“We need to be aware of these heart disease risks so we’re not caught by surprise 10 to 20 years down the road,” Weinberg said.

Suppogu agreed. “Medical professionals should emphasize that heart health is a lifelong priority and prevention should begin early. Encourage girls and women to establish healthy habits, understand their cardiovascular risk factors, and maintain regular checkups, even when they feel healthy.”.

“Women’s heart health has a unique constellation of risk factors and manifestations that are shaped by biological transitions that vary across a woman’s lifetime,” noted Shah.

The second report is a science advisory that recommends a comprehensive plan for women’s cardiovascular care.

In it, the authors call for a system that “integrates assessment of hormonal, psychosocial, and cardiovascular health across life stages.”.

They propose a “national infrastructure” of centers that would coordinate clinical care, education, training, research, and community engagement around women’s heart health.

Industry observers note that “These centers can reduce fragmentation, enhance earlier risk identification, and expand opportunities to increase representation of women in clinical research,” the authors wrote. “In doing so, they offer a bold opportunity for a scalable and equitable model to improve cardiovascular health for all women.”.

To illustrate their point, the authors noted that only about 60% of women with hypertensive disorders during pregnancy in the United States have a follow-up visit with a healthcare professional about their condition within the first 6 months after giving birth.

“Given that pregnancy is a cardiovascular stress test and hypertensive disorders of pregnancy are risk-enhancing factors for long-term [cardiovascular disease] risk, this represents a major missed opportunity to address cardiovascular risk,” the authors wrote.

“Pregnancy and the postpartum period are notable windows into cardiovascular health throughout the life course,” mentioned William Grobman, MD, the vice-chair of the writing group for these reports and a professor of obstetrics and gynecology at The Warren Alpert Medical School of Brown University in Providence, Rhode Island, in the press release.

“An adverse pregnancy outcome can unmask increased cardiovascular risk, and that information should guide care well beyond pregnancy,” he continued.

The third report is a scientific statement that suggests a “consensus guideline for the female-specific prevention and management of cardiovascular disease.”.

In it, the authors state that there is “growing recognition that the optimal prevention and management of cardiovascular disease in girls and women requires attention to sex-specific considerations relevant to the interconnected domains of hormonal, psychosocial, and cardiovascular health across the life course.”.

The authors note several age-related warning signs of heart issues. These are spelled out in the AHA press release.

According to recent reports, females comprise around half the population, and their cardiovascular health “must be a part of everyday care across medicine,” remarked Mariell Jessup, MD, the chief science and medical officer of the American Heart Association, in the press release. “These publications give clinicians and health systems a shared foundation for recognizing risk throughout a woman’s life.”.

In a scientific statement published in February 2026, the AHA projected that 60% of females in the United States will have at least one type of cardiovascular disease by 2050.

The organization also predicted that 25% of U.S. women will have diabetes and 60% will have obesity by that year if current trends continue.

According to recent reports, the authors of that report listed several steps they stated could reverse these trends. Among them:.

Experts say women can also take action on their own to reduce their risks. Suppogu suggests the following:.

These recommendations can also be found in the AHA’s Life’s Essential 8 tips for a healthy heart.

“Most importantly, we need to educate women that heart disease is not inevitable, and early intervention can help prevent it and improve long-term health,” Suppogu remarked.

According to recent reports, weinberg advised women to include plenty of fruits and vegetables and a minimal amount of meat in their daily diet. She said that women should have regular check-ups with their doctor, and that adopting a healthy lifestyle doesn’t have to be complicated.

Khan stated women’s health is a community effort. “All girls and women deserve more healthy years to live their fullest lives,” she said in the press release.

Industry observers note that “Advancing women’s health is a responsibility we all share. This investment improves not only women’s health but also the health of their families and their communities.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A week after Waymo was banned from operating on California freeways, the autonomous rideshare service has now paused freeway operations across the United States.

The California-based startup declared the temporary pause on Wednesday, November 18, although it actually began on November 11. Normally, Waymo offers freeway service in the San Francisco Bay Area, Los Angeles, Phoenix, Miami, and Austin. The Associated Press cited a Waymo statement saying it is temporarily restricting “commercial freeway rides in all markets where we operate that service.” However, Waymo said it would continue freeway testing with trained autonomous specialists at the wheel.

It is not immediately clear when the freeway pause will be lifted. California initiated the ban last week after multiple incidents of Waymo vehicles driving into construction zones or disobeying orders from law enforcement; the state DMV noted an incident on November 5 and another on November 6 drove the regulatory agency to ban autonomous freeway operations.

Recent findings suggest that “The Department determined that Waymo’s driverless freeway operations pose an imminent hazard to public safety due to recurring incursions by its vehicles into active construction zones where construction workers, vehicles and equipment are present,” California DMV spokesperson Jonathan Groveman stated to the Associated Press. “The Department determined that Waymo’s driverless freeway operations pose an imminent hazard to public safety due to recurring incursions by its vehicles into active construction zones where construction workers, vehicles and equipment are present.”.

Road & Track has reached out to Waymo for comment, and will patch the story if we learn more.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, tesla has opened its first Semi Megacharger in Texas, an 8-stall station in Mesquite on the east side of Dallas. With it, Tesla’s map now lists 7 public Megacharger sites and 44 stalls for its electric truck.

That’s progress. But with six weeks left in 2026, it’s less than a fifth of the 37 sites Tesla planned to have open this year.

Tesla Charging unveiled the newly introduced station on X on Tuesday night with its usual one-liner and a photo of the stalls at sunset:.

Latest Tesla Megacharger: Mesquite, TX (8 stalls) https://t.co/UsCFMyCjo7 pic.twitter.com/W4G1e2BHkb.

Tesla’s map lists the site at 2175 S Town East Blvd in Mesquite, with eight Megachargers rated at up to 1.2 MW each.

Texas is where Tesla has the most riding on this network. When Tesla added 64 Megacharger locations to its map in February, Texas got 19 of the 66 planned sites, more than any other state. Mesquite is the first of them to go live, and several other Dallas–Fort Worth sites are still marked “coming soon.”.

The Pilot truck stop rollout hasn’t reached Texas either. When Pilot opened its first Megacharger in Georgia in October, it named a Flying J in Fort Stockton, Texas, as one of the next sites. It’s still not live on Tesla’s map.

According to recent reports, tesla also isn’t alone in DFW. Greenlane, the truck charging joint venture between Daimler Truck, NextEra and BlackRock, announced high-power sites in Dallas and Houston in May, open to any electric truck with CCS and MCS connectors. Tesla now has a station operating in the metro.

Here’s every public Megacharger right now live on Tesla’s map:.

That’s 7 sites and 44 stalls in four states. When we counted in early October, there were four customer-facing sites with 26 stalls. Tulare opened the same week, Hodgkins came on November 10, and now Mesquite.

So Tesla is adding a site roughly every two weeks.

Tesla also runs private Megachargers for its own fleet at Giga Nevada and in Carson, California, and it sells Megachargers to fleets and depot operators through its business program. Forum Mobility switched on two at the Port of Long Beach earlier this month. None of those count toward the public network that Semi buyers without their own depot rely on.

It has been revealed that tesla’s Q4 2025 shareholder report showed about 37 Megacharger sites for 2026. Semi program lead Dan Priestley has mentioned Tesla wants 46 by early 2027.

To me this seems like good progress, sure it's not right on time with their ambitious goal, but they are executing on their charging network and I'm sure more sites will keep opening.

To hit 37, Tesla would need to open 30 more sites in the next 43 days. At the current pace, it ends the year with around 10.

Industry observers note that pilot remarked in October that nine more of its sites were under construction, so a late burst is possible. But it would have to be a very significant one.

It has been revealed that and the trucks are starting to show up. Tesla launched volume production of the Semi in September at a Nevada factory it says can build 50,000 trucks a year, and it remarked last week that Chicago’s first 50 Semis are en route for delivery, a day after Hodgkins opened. Significant fleets like that customer are installing their own depot chargers anyway, and most Semi charging will happen there. The public network is what lets a Semi leave its home region.

#132553. Before public bathrooms, women were kept on a ‘urinary leash.’ Then department stores changed everything.

Before public bathrooms, women were kept on a ‘urinary leash.’ Then department stores changed everything.

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1733 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Popsci

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that what’s the weirdest thing you learned this week?
  • Today’s episode features the three hosts of Vanity Veritas, a delightful podcast about the history of beauty.
  • In a recent development, for most of modern human history, a woman’s range of motion in the world was limited by how long she could hold her pee.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that what’s the weirdest thing you learned this week? Well, whatever it is, we promise you’ll have an even weirder answer if you listen to PopSci’s hit podcast. The Weirdest Thing I Learned This Week hits Spotify, YouTube, Apple, and everywhere else you listen to podcasts every-other Wednesday morning. It’s your upcoming favorite source for the strangest science-adjacent facts, figures, and Wikipedia spirals the editors of Popular Science can muster. If you like the stories in this post, we guarantee you’ll love the show.

Today’s episode features the three hosts of Vanity Veritas, a delightful podcast about the history of beauty. VV’s co-host Kristina dove into the history of public toilets—and the longstanding lack thereof, at least for women.

In a recent development, for most of modern human history, a woman’s range of motion in the world was limited by how long she could hold her pee. Historians call this the “urinary leash.”.

You might be wondering how this could possibly be a gendered issue, given the universality of the need to urinate. There was almost certainly a time when humans of all types could duck behind trees (or not) and relieve themselves with pretty similar levels of comfort and ease. But by the time Ancient Romans were using public latrines in the 2nd century BC, women of good standing weren’t supposed to go anywhere near them.

Sources indicate that so when “monkey closets”—the first public flush toilets—debuted at London’s Great Exhibition in 1851, women didn’t benefit much. Some men thought women would be (or maybe should be) too embarrassed to enter a public restroom, so they were often excluded. And sometimes, if bathrooms were installed for women, they were sabotaged by men who took offense. By the time municipal toilets started popping up, they were often isolated and unsupervised, which meant even women willing to break the taboo had to worry about safety concerns. A woman on the go might come across a genteel lounge reserved for ladies, but they were designed for swooning in and kept decidedly toilet-free.

Sources indicate that ergo the “urinary leash”: you could only travel as far as your bladder allowed. That’s about two to five hours, if you don’t want to put your health at risk. Keep in mind that this was before cars, so a trip across the city would easily take up a good chunk of that time.

The options when you were away from home were pretty grim. You could take a wide-stance squat over a grate, if you were desperate. On the one hand, bloomer crotches were split down the middle to allow for easy evacuation. On the other hand, a woman would have four to eight layers of skirts to try to protect from backsplash. Wealthy ladies might use a fancy porcelain urinal called a “bourdaloue.” (Fun fact: Many antique dealers now sell these as gravy boats.).

According to recent reports, the solution? Department stores. Obviously the actual solution was just providing women with decent public bathrooms, but no one bothered to do so until the owner of Marshall Field’s in Chicago realized that safe, clean toilets would draw women to the store—and allow them to shop for longer. Their luxurious facilities opened in 1907, and not a moment too soon. They featured extra-wide stalls (for bustles, naturally) and a staffed nursery.

In a recent development, harry Selfridge, who rose up in the ranks at Marshall Field’s before striking out on his own, later took the idea to London when he opened his eponymous department store there. But he actually upped the ante and added hot running water, telephones, writing desks, and more. (Editor’s note: Please bring back department store coworking spaces.) Marshall Field’s and Selfridge’s weren’t doing this for the sake of women’s lib; a safe place to pee meant women could spend more time out of the house, which meant spending more money. But these spaces did set a precedent that helped activists push for women’s restrooms in more places, and they also made it easier for suffragists to hang out and strategize. In 2023, Selfridge’s celebrated its place in the history of peeing in public with Exhibition, an artwork by Gray Wielebinski reflecting on the rich cultural significance of communal bathrooms—and the threats they still face today.

In a recent development, these days, access to public bathrooms is nowhere near as widespread as it should be. That’s especially true for trans people, who have been subjected to a wave of state laws attempting to restrict which restrooms they can use. As the history of public toilets—and the dreaded urinary leash—should remind us, a bathroom isn’t “just a bathroom,” and restrictions on their use have a chilling effect on autonomy.

For more on the massive cultural impact of department stores, check out Vanity Veritas.

Because this week’s episode featured three special guests, I decided to keep my fact short. Cockney rhyming slang—a code that came out of East London in the 19th century—is not a subject I have a lot to say about, but it is something I want to make sure you know exists. Contrary to popular belief, there’s no strong evidence that this cheeky and cryptic lexicon arose to facilitate criminal acts. But whatever fueled its creation, it’s persisted in various subcultures to this day. The system works like this: pick a phrase that rhymes with the word you’re actually referring to, then drop the part that actually rhymes. Tricky? Yes. Whimsical? Very.

If you’ve ever wondered why that fart sound you make with your lips is called a “raspberry,” you have Cockney Rhyming Slang to thank. Fart rhymes with raspberry tart, which then gets shortened to raspberry. Things get stranger when you move into double and triple rhyme territory. “Bottle and glass” meant arse, so “bottle” did too. Then “bottle” got rhymed with Aristotle, which got shortened to “Aris,” which got rhymed with plaster of Paris. Congratulations, “plaster” now means butt.

You can check out a full dictionary of Cockney rhyming slang—with folks weighing in to confirm words or mark them as made-up “Mockney”.

Recent findings suggest that opera diva Maria Callas famously shed her weight with the help of a tapeworm, just like loads of Victorian women did. Right? Well, not quite. In fact, the truth is probably even more disgusting.

Actual opera singer (and Rachel’s sister!) Chelsea Feltman did a deep dive on Callas for Vanity Veritas a while back, so she dove into the nitty gritty of the tapeworm myth for this week’s Weirdest Thing.

It has been revealed that maria Callas really did drop a troubling amount of weight over the course of 18 months in the 1950s, and she really did have a beef tapeworm. But according to a 2022 review in Parasitologia, the idea that the tapeworm was her go-to weightloss hack is actually backwards. She most likely caught the tapeworm as the result of the high-protein, rare-meat diet she favored for weight loss. Sources disagree on whether Callas ever infected herself on purpose, but the fact remains that this parasite was not a diet hack: Even a five-meter beef tapeworm wouldn’t cause much weight loss, though it could definitely leave you vitamin-deficient. Some tapeworms can even form cysts in your brain.

In a recent development, the idea of popping worm pills popped up in December 1912, when the Washington Post reported that a society woman in Peoria had paid for two suspicious capsules that her husband then analyzed. Inside, he mentioned, he found tapeworm parts. The woman, the vendor, and the government agent were never named, which strongly suggests this story was probably at least kinda made up. The next day, the surgeon general said he’d never seen such a pill, and the Hygienic Laboratory’s director called it the wildest story he’d heard in a while. The legend kept growing anyway, with a bigger price tag in an Ohio paper in 1914 and a comic-strip “diet doctor” with wriggling capsules in 1927. It may even trace back to an 1899 Indiana medicine-show man arrested for giving patients artificial tapeworms to “pass” as proof his cure worked. Mostly, this seems to be a cultural meme that served to mock vain, silly women.

According to recent reports, unfortunately, this hasn’t stopped real people from trying to take advantage of this fake historical trend. In 2013, Iowa’s state medical director warned about a patient who’d swallowed a tapeworm they bought online.

(If you’re looking for the picture of the cheese-baited tapeworm-catching device, here you go.).

According to recent reports, in the early 20th century, about 100 American women died of cervical cancer every day. The only diagnostic test was a biopsy, and by the time women experienced symptoms it was usually too late for anyone to help them. The test that changed it all came from a Greek immigrant who never set out to find it.

George Papanicolaou moved to Newly introduced York in 1913 and drifted through odd jobs, including playing violin in a restaurant and a stint as a famously bad carpet salesman. He finally landed a lab gig under Charles Stockard, a prominent eugenicist who wanted to understand human reproduction as a means of better controlling it (ugh). There, Papanicolaou found he could swab live guinea pigs for cervical cells instead of doing invasive biopsies. He wondered whether the method would work on humans.

According to recent reports, his wife Mary became (human) guinea pig number one. For 21 years, she gave a sample almost every day—roughly 7,600 pap smears—while also staining slides, recruiting friends, and later training the technicians who read results. George introduced her to people as “my wife and victim.”.

In 1925 George spotted cancer cells in a hospital sample. He took that historic discovery to a 1928 conference sponsored by eugenicists, where he presented blurry slides to doctors who preferred the biopsy method over his smear concept. Things… didn’t go well.

It has been revealed that it took Stockard’s death, a new boss for George, a collaboration testing more than 3,000 women, and artist Hashime Murayama’s vivid cell illustrations to turn the test into a medical landmark. By the late 1950s, women were lining up around the block for pap smears, and US cervical cancer deaths fell by about 70 percent.

Amflow debuts its first city e-bikes, packing huge torque and serious smart tech

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that amflow has made a name for itself in the electric mountain bike world with its high-performance Avinox-powered machines, but now the company is bringing that same technology to a decidedly more urban environment. The newly unveiled Amflow UE Carbon series marks the brand’s first move into the commuter e-bike market, combining a lightweight carbon fiber frame, powerful mid-drive motor, and a surprisingly long list of smart features designed for everyday riding.

And while these might look like fairly conventional step-through city bikes at first glance, there’s some seriously impressive technology hiding beneath those clean lines.

The newly introduced Amflow UE series comes in two versions, the UE Carbon and the higher-end UE Carbon Pro, both built around a full-carbon fiber frame weighing just 2.35 kg (5.2 lb).

The complete bike weighs as little as 20.9 kg (46 lb), which is fairly impressive considering the amount of hardware Amflow has packed into it, including front suspension, a suspension dropper seatpost, integrated lighting, and cargo racks.

Both models use the Avinox M2 mid-drive motor, which delivers up to 125 Nm of torque. That’s an enormous amount of torque for a city bike, and should make short work of steep hills, especially when carrying groceries or other cargo. And to put things into perspective, a lot of city e-bikes have barely 60 Nm for torque, so Amflow is knocking it out of the park for urban power.

A removable 600 Wh battery provides a claimed maximum range of 132 km (82 miles) in the lowest power assist mode, while fast charging can refill the battery in just 2 hours and 23 minutes.

The bikes also feature Avinox’s intelligent traction control system and a latest Auto Boost function that automatically provides additional assistance when the system detects demanding conditions, such as accelerating from a stop or climbing a steep hill.

In other words, riders get much of the sophisticated motor technology developed for high-performance electric mountain bikes, but in a package designed for commuting to work or picking up groceries.

The bike is listed as weighing 20.9 kg (46 lb), though that figure conveniently excludes the front and rear racks, mudguards, pedals, kickstand, bike lock, bottle cage, and chainguard. So figure a few extra pounds for all of that gear, and you’re in the right ballpark.

The main difference between the two models is their drivetrain.

The higher-end UE Carbon Pro ($3,899) uses a customized three-speed electronically shifted internally geared hub paired with a Gates carbon belt drive. That should make it particularly appealing to commuters who want a quiet, clean, low-maintenance setup without worrying about chain lubrication or derailleur adjustments.

The more affordable UE Carbon ($3,499) instead uses a 10-speed electronic derailleur developed with TRP.

Both models support automatic shifting, allowing the bike to handle gear changes without requiring the rider to constantly think about them.

Amflow has also gone fairly wild with the technology integration.

There’s a 1.4-inch touchscreen display mounted on the handlebars, a wireless phone charging mount offering 15W wireless charging or 20W USB-C charging, and integrated lighting with automatic low-light activation and brake-sensing functionality.

The bikes even include a hardened steel frame lock on the rear wheel, Apple Find My integration, and a Lost Mode feature that can lock down certain components if the bike is stolen.

Apple Watch connectivity allows riders to check their bike’s status and unlock it, while heart-rate-based assistance can automatically adjust motor output to help riders maintain a target heart rate zone.

Some of these features, like the security and tracking, are immediately effective for nearly all riders, while other high-tech features like the heart rate-based pedal assist can provide even more functionality for niche riders looking to bridge the gap between riding for transportation and riding for fitness.

Of course, all the fancy technology in the world doesn’t mean much if a commuter bike can’t handle everyday errands.

Fortunately, Amflow appears to have taken the practical side seriously.

The bikes feature a low step-through frame, upright riding position, 65 mm suspension fork, and a suspension dropper seatpost offering 125 mm of height adjustment and approximately 30 mm of suspension travel.

The 26×2.0-inch Maxxis tires should also provide a comfortable ride over less-than-perfect city streets.

There’s a front rack rated for 20 kg (44 lb) and a rear rack rated for 27 kg (59.5 lb), with the latter supporting the MIK HD mounting system for compatible accessories, including child seats.

The standard frame is designed to accommodate riders from 155 to 190 cm (5’1” to 6’3”), while a smaller version for riders down to 140 cm (4’7”) is expected in 2027.

I’ve been impressed with the technology coming out of the Avinox ecosystem, and it’s exciting to see that technology finally make its way into a more practical city-focused electric bicycle.

It has been revealed that as much as I love high-performance electric mountain bikes, the reality is that most people aren’t spending their mornings bombing down mountain trails. They’re commuting to work, dropping kids off at school, and running errands.

And that’s where electric bicycles can make an even bigger difference.

According to recent reports, the Amflow UE series seems to take a refreshingly comprehensive approach to urban riding. The powerful motor is nice, but I’m arguably more interested in the belt drive, integrated security, cargo capacity, automatic shifting, and built-in phone charging.

Those are the kinds of features that can make an electric bicycle genuinely easier to live with every day. And as someone who actually commutes with an e-bike each day as my main form of transportation, these bikes are really speaking to me!

It has been revealed that if you ask me, it’s great to see another high-performance e-bike manufacturer recognizing that the future of electric bicycles isn’t just about riding farther and faster on trails. It’s also about making everyday transportation better for the less exciting type of riding, too.

Latest Update: Mathematicians make a breakthrough in 174-year-old problem

💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, while mathematicians technically solved a nearly 175-year-old theorem known as the Four-Color Problem in 1976, the problem continues to vex researchers.
  • The underlying conceit to the Four-Color Problem is deceptively straightforward.
  • According to recent reports, it took more than 85 years until a full proof arrived—a particularly notable moment, since it was also the first major theorem proven by a computer program.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, while mathematicians technically solved a nearly 175-year-old theorem known as the Four-Color Problem in 1976, the problem continues to vex researchers. For some in the field, their fascination with the perniciously complex concept runs so deep, that they liken their obsession to a lingering disease. But after a decade of analysis, an international team of mathematicians has made the first major breakthrough in the ongoing Four-Color Problem saga in 30 years. At this year’s Foundations of Computer Science (FOCS) conference, investigators laid out the optimal, most efficient algorithm that solves the Four-Color Problem.

The underlying conceit to the Four-Color Problem is deceptively straightforward. In 1852, 19th century English mathematician Francis Guthrie posited that you only need a quartet of hues to fill every border-enclosed region on a map. Think all territories, regions, states, and nations filled in with only four colors. The first proof was introduced in 1879, and seemed solid for 11 years. That is, until Guthrie’s colleagues found an error in the calculations.

According to recent reports, it took more than 85 years until a full proof arrived—a particularly notable moment, since it was also the first major theorem proven by a computer program. However, many in the mathematical community took problem with the digital discovery after having difficulty verifying it themselves.

In a recent development, A more accessible proof arrived in 1997, but even then, the algorithmic system became painfully slow as sample maps grew larger. A handful of mathematicians around the world have pondered newly introduced approaches to the problem ever since—including University of Copenhagen computer scientist Mikkel Thorup, who likens his interest to a “four-color disease.”.

“I would guess that at least 1,000 mathematicians have caught the four-color disease, spending months trying to make it work but never quite succeeding,” Thorup remarked in a university profile. “It is the disease people have suffered from since 1852.”.

According to recent reports, it took years, but Thorup and his colleagues made progress after uncovering a novel detail regarding map-like surfaces known as planar graphs. The researchers realized these graphs feature many more reducible arrangements than experts previously assumed. This provided them a much more discreet set of starting points.

According to recent reports, “Think of reducible configurations as handles you can grab hold on to start four-coloring,” added study co-author and Technical University of Denmark (DTU) mathematician Carsten Thomassen. “We show that graphs do not contain just one handle, but an astonishing number of them. Nobody knew that before.”.

According to recent reports, instead of one or two handles in a graph, the team could now identify many more handles throughout any given map. This allowed them to simultaneously begin filling regions with four colors, which exponentially quickened the overall process. Thomassen noted this boosted their algorithm from quadratic time (where calculation speed increases proportionally to the square of an input size) to linear time.

Industry observers note that “This means that if a map contains ten times as many regions, the computation only becomes about ten times slower. With the previous algorithm, it would have become about 100 times slower,” he added.

Sources indicate that but does this really change anything beyond theoretical mathematics? According to researchers, the answer is a resounding “yes.”.

It has been revealed that “The remarkable thing is that because there are so many handles, the idea can also be applied to other kinds of surfaces besides a flat map,” mentioned Thorup. “For example, surfaces with holes, such as a swim ring or a piece of…cheese.”.

Okay, so the implications may be somewhat subtle for most people’s day-to-day lives. That doesn’t change the fact that mathematicians finally worked through symptoms of their disease for the first time in 30 years. As to why Thorup and his colleagues spent a decade on a theorem whose major immediate implications are “cheese,” he had a relatively succinct explanation.

Industry observers note that “Because mathematicians are slightly crazy. Most of what mathematicians work on consists of very nerdy questions,” he mentioned. “We become obsessed with this type of problem because it challenges the human intellect. And if we find the answer, we’ll probably also find answers to other mathematical puzzles.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Presumably as a way of marching ever forward towards its (alleged) 100 million player goal for Battlefield 6, EA has announced that the multiplayer shooter will be getting its first free trial later this month.

This is, of course, specifically for players to sample the core, paid component of the game, as the recently rolled out Redsec remains free-to-play. Redsec, however, offers modes like battle royale and Gauntlet, which aren’t quite the traditional Battlefield experience.

The Battlefield 6 trial arrives next Tuesday, November 25. It will run for one week, ending the following Tuesday, December 2. The trial will be available on all platforms, but won’t include all content from the full game.

In a recent development, instead, players will have access to three of the game’s maps and five of its modes. Siege of Cairo will be there alongside Season 1’s two new maps: Eastwood, and Blackwell Fields. It’s not the strongest line-up of maps, considering Eastwood is already cut from the larger Fort Lyndon battle royale map that Redsec players should be quite familiar with, but it’s something.

In a recent development, as for modes, you can pick from Conquest, Breakthrough, Sabotage, and Team Deathmatch. Battlefield Studios didn’t say what the fifth mode is going to be, but a dedicated blog post with more information is set to arrive next week.

Beyond the trial's content itself, the timing is certainly great. Battlefield 6 just received one of its biggest patches, kicking off the second phase of its first season. So far this season, we’ve seen two fresh maps, several new weapons - but more importantly, solutions to problems the game’s had since launch, as well as fixes to longstanding bugs.

Sources indicate that the miserable XP progression Battlefield 6 introduced with is far more tolerable. Challenges and Assignments are much easier to understand and actually finish. The often maligned weapon dispersion has been toned down. Some of the wildest vehicle bugs have been fixed. And Portal has a host of experiences that go beyond just bot farms.

In essence, Battlefield 6 feels like its reached its 1.0 status, which makes this a great entry point for new players, even if the trial could've used more of the game's better maps.

Recent findings suggest that it’s been two years since Lego and Formula 1 first partnered up to translate the excitement of the grand prix grid into tiny, plastic, painful-to-step-on brick form. But while the race cars were a realistic low-polygon tribute to the life-size real things, the minifigures that accompanied them were fairly generic. Until now, that is, because the upcoming Lego Speed Champions lineup features all 11 teams on the 2026 grid and all 22 full-time drivers, rendered with realistic driving suits and customized hair.

It has been revealed that announced at the 2026 Las Vegas Grand Prix against a backdrop of several giant minifigures and a full complement of Lego-clad go-karts (now updated with neon LED light strips for the full Vegas experience), this next batch of Speed Champions sets will go on sale March 1, 2027. That makes for plenty of time to build all 11 before the first race of the season in Bahrain, although it’s also yet another thing to wait for during the off-season.

Arvid Lindblad, driver for the Visa Cash App Racing Bulls Team, made at appearance at Lego’s press announcement, and posed with both his large and small Lego likenesses. Asked about his thoughts on the result, the British driver said: “Awesome, nailed it. They got the hair perfect,” adding that, “I’ve always loved Legos, though I never imagined having my own minifigure.”.

Recent findings suggest that and speaking of hair, yes, the Valteri Bottas minifigure is rocking a mullet. Each plastic hairpiece was approved by the respective drivers. “When we pitched the the hairstyles to the teams and the drivers, they absolutely loved it,” noted Will Thorogood, the Lego designer who led this effort. “They all thought it was as funny as we did.”.

It has been revealed that another key part of bringing out the driver’s personality is the helmets, which are “far more detailed than any helmet we've ever done before with the with the Lego production,” according to Thorogood. Lando Norris’s helmet, for example, “has all the blob details on it” as well as a minifigure Easter egg hidden in the design. Each driver also comes with two facial expressions on opposite sides of the minfigure head; Charles Leclerc’s visage is either relaxed in sunglasses or a more serious grimace, both with the Ferrari driver’s stubbled mustache and goatee.

The cars themselves reflect the new regulations and, says Thorogood, “as you look closely, you'll see every single one is built completely differently to capture all the aero details and principles that each of the teams has employed.” These too feature several Easter eggs for Lego fans, such as suspension wishbones made from wizard wands and rear diffuser strakes made from minifigure meat cleavers.

According to recent reports, measuring 7.5 inches long and 2.5 inches wide, the Speed Champions sets will be priced at $29.99 when they go on sale next year. More photos and details are viewable now on the Speed Champions section of the Lego Website.

It has been revealed that executive Editor Mike Austin has worked as a writer, editor, and occasional video host across titles such as Car and Driver, Autoblog, Popular Mechanics, and Hemmings (plus a few more). Prior to joining Road & Track he finally put his engineering degrees to use as an EV analyst. His personal cars skew slightly oddball, including a 1991 Honda Beat, 2001 Volkswagen Eurovan, 1987 Alfa Romeo Spider, and 2007 Saab 9-3 wagon.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Charis Bridger-Staatz, PhD, a senior research fellow at UCL, led the study.
  • It has been revealed that the findings can apply to Americans because British and U.S.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that losing weight in your 50s, even a modest amount, may help protect your heart health later in life, according to fresh research.Adults who lost weight in their early 50s saw their blood pressure, “good” cholesterol and inflammation change at about the same rate as adults who stayed at a healthy weight, according to a study from researchers at University College London and the University of Glasgow.Adults who gained weight in their early 50s saw those same measures worsen faster by their early 60s, the researchers reported. The authors posted the study on a research-sharing website on September 4. Other scientists have not yet peer-reviewed the work.

Charis Bridger-Staatz, PhD, a senior research fellow at UCL, led the study. She told Healthline the main takeaway for adults over 50 was that “it’s not too late to try and do things that are going to improve your health.”Nearly half of U.S. adults ages 40 to 59 had obesity from 2021 to 2023, the highest rate of any adult age group, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC). Among all U.S. adults, around 31.7% were overweight, according to the CDC.

It has been revealed that the findings can apply to Americans because British and U.S. adults share similar weight patterns, said Solveig Cunningham, PhD, a professor of global health at Emory University’s Rollins School of Public Health. Cunningham, who was not involved in the research, told Healthline that Americans tend to gain weight across adulthood.

“By the time you get into your 50s, close to the majority of Americans already have obesity. Many others have overweight,” she noted.The World Health Organization (WHO) calls obesity a chronic disease. Healthcare professionals diagnose overweight and obesity using a person’s weight and height, or body mass index (BMI).

Bridger-Staatz said the team set out to learn who lost weight and kept it off before GLP-1 weight loss medications became available, and whether that weight loss improved health over time.

Industry observers note that she mentioned researchers had long assumed that “once people had become overweight or developed obesity, people didn’t really lose weight and certainly not sustained it.”The team also asked, she said, “can we try and say something positive about health that isn’t just this kind of like doom and gloom?”The researchers used the British 1958 National Child Development Study, which has followed about 17,500 people born during one week in 1958. Of those, 6,309 took part in a health check in their early 60s, according to the report.The team compared each person’s highest weight between ages 23 and 42 with their weight between ages 50 and 55. Researchers sorted people by whether they gained or lost more than 5% of their body weight and kept the change. For a 200-pound person, 5% equals 10 pounds.To track heart health, the team compared blood tests and blood pressure readings at ages 44 and 62 with those of people who maintained a healthy weight.“We know everyone’s heart health is kind of going to get a little bit worse over that time because you are aging and that’s expected,” Bridger-Staatz said. The question, she said, was, “Does it slow the rate at which people’s heart health is getting worse?”.

Weight loss slowed the decline in heart health for people who were overweight and for people with obesity, according to the report.People who were overweight and lost weight had the strongest positive results. By age 62, their body fat-to-lean tissue ratio matched that of the healthy-weight group. The authors wrote that differences in body fat may partly explain why weight changes affected heart health.People with obesity who lost weight had less body fat at 62 than people in the other obesity groups, according to the report.Sudhakara Chennareddy, MD, prevention cardiologist in the Center for Cardiovascular Prevention, Metabolism and Lipids at Georgia Heart Institute, told Healthline those results are what he’d expect. He was not involved in the research.“Even losing 5% has beneficial effects on the cardiovascular side effects,” he stated. Long-term blood sugar was the exception. For people with obesity who lost weight, it rose more than in the healthy-weight group, though the authors reported that the result was not statistically significant.

Sources indicate that A 2025 study of more than 15,000 U.S. adults, published in Endocrinology, Diabetes & Metabolism, found that adults who had previously had obesity tended to have higher blood sugar than those who had never had it, even after their BMI dropped.

It has been revealed that “It’s not the patient’s fault… We need to treat this one like any other chronic disease, like we treat hypertension or we treat diabetes,” Chennareddy remarked.Compared with the healthy-weight group, people who gained weight in their early 50s had faster increases in blood pressure, blood fats, and inflammation, and declines in “good” cholesterol. Obesity is a chronic metabolic disease that leads to inflammation in the body, which can raise the risk of heart attack and stroke and worsen cholesterol levels, Chennareddy said. “The more weight they gain, they develop prediabetes and diabetes and fatty liver disease as well,” he said.These changes were largest for people who developed obesity or already had obesity and gained more weight, the researchers reported. This group also saw faster increases in long-term blood sugar levels.About 37% of participants gained more than 5% of their body weight in their early 50s. Only about 6% lost weight and kept it off, according to the study.“To me, that’s sort of the stronger message,” Cunningham said of the findings. Her advice for adults in their 50s is to avoid gaining weight.

People with obesity who lost and then gained the weight back saw faster drops in “good” cholesterol and faster rises in inflammation and long-term blood sugar.

By age 62, they weighed slightly less, on average, than people whose obesity remained steady, according to the report’s data. They also carried more body fat and had more inflammation.Weight cycling can do more harm than steady weight, Chennareddy noted. He gave the example of someone who gains 20 pounds, loses 30 and then gains 20 again. “That is even more detrimental,” he said.When people lose weight, the body slows its resting metabolism, he said. When the weight comes back, “most of the weight they gain is fat, not muscle,” he said. Even someone who loses and regains 5% to 7% of their body weight may end up with slightly less muscle and more fat, he said.Some research has shown that weight fluctuation is associated with a higher risk of high blood pressure and cardiovascular disease-related death.

The study’s weight changes took place between about 2008 and 2013, according to the study’s timeline.

According to recent reports, wegovy, a GLP-1 medication for weight management, released in the United Kingdom in September 2023, according to the UK Department of Health and Social Care.Cunningham said the weight-cycling findings raised questions for people who take GLP-1 medications. She said drugmakers’ own data show that “once you get off of those, your weight is going to go right back to where it was before, possibly even worse.”That could create the same up-and-down pattern, Cunningham said. She added that researchers don’t yet know “what happens in the really long term” for people who take these medications.

Industry observers note that the study revealed links between weight changes and heart health and cannot prove that weight changes caused the results, according to the authors. They wrote that the small number of people who lost weight made those results less precise.Bridger-Staatz also noted the team did not look at why or how people lost weight.

Industry observers note that cunningham mentioned adults lose muscle and bone mass with age, and that the loss is especially pronounced for women in their 50s and older. “Maintaining muscles and maintaining bones is so, so important,” she said.Staying active helps people keep muscle, even without weight loss, Cunningham said. “Even a little bit of activity…just keep moving,” she said.GLP-1 medications work best as part of a “comprehensive proposal,” Chennareddy said. With his patients, he said he recommends continuous improvement rather than setting a goal to lose a specific amount of weight within a set period.Patients who treat weight loss as “a gradual process” do better long term, he said.“The most important thing is not to do fad diets,” Chennareddy said.For people losing weight, Chennareddy recommended:.

Anyone considering changes to their weight can talk with a healthcare professional about their weight history and goals.

#132547. Why Does Life Feel Absurd?

Why Does Life Feel Absurd?

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (811 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Psychologytoday

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Posted November 22, 2026 | Reviewed by Jessica Schrader.
  • “MOST people feel on occasion that life is absurd, and some feel it vividly and continually” is how Thomas Nagel opens his paper "The Absurd," yet "they could not really explain why life is absurd.
  • It has been revealed that what then is the absurd?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Posted November 22, 2026 | Reviewed by Jessica Schrader.

“MOST people feel on occasion that life is absurd, and some feel it vividly and continually” is how Thomas Nagel opens his paper "The Absurd," yet "they could not really explain why life is absurd. Why then do they provide a natural expression for the sense that it is?” This is why I've recently published an academic article on the topic.

It has been revealed that what then is the absurd? As Albert Camus is most often associated with the term the absurd, I will begin with his account. He begins by illustrating the common uses of the word absurd and gives the example of a virtuous man, who we accuse of desiring his sister. Naturally, he would respond in shock: “That is absurd!” Thereby appealing to the “contradictory” and “impossible” notion of the accusation, like a man attacking a group of gunmen with a sword. The intention of the action clashes with the harsh reality, thereby rendering the whole endeavor absurd. For Camus, the “absurd is born of this confrontation between the human need [for meaning and reason] and the unreasonable silence of the world.”.

Recent findings suggest that the feeling of the absurd therefore stems from two realizations taken together. First, man’s realization that life is meaningless and the universe purposeless; and secondly, man’s desire for meaning and purpose. The absurd is the futile search for meaning. It is neither existential nihilism that is absurd, nor the human search for meaning, but the comparison, the conflict, that arises between them.

Let us now take a look at an analytical philosopher, i.e., Thomas Nagel and his paper “The Absurd." Nagel, too, starts from the notion of the absurd in ordinary life, giving a similar analysis to Camus’, stating that it “includes a conspicuous discrepancy between pretension or aspiration and reality," like someone giving a complex speech on a vote that has already been cast. A philosophical notion of absurdity, in contrast to the feeling of absurdity, however, must according to Nagel lie in “something universal-some respect in which pretension and reality inevitably clash for us all” and that is a “collision between the seriousness with which we take our lives and the perpetual possibility of regarding everything about which we are serious as arbitrary, or open to doubt.”.

In a recent development, as one might argue goes, “why struggle, if the struggle doesn’t amount to anything?” This question is unique for humans, in that only they have the ability to take a step back and look at themselves from a grander point of view, which is seemingly impossible for animals. From this perspective, our lives must appear “sobering and comical.” As Nagel claims:.

We step back to find that the whole system of justification and criticism, which controls our choices and supports our claims to rationality, rests on responses and habits that we never question, that we should not know how to defend without circularity, and to which we shall continue to adhere even after they are called into question.

Our aims and goals must from this perspective appear arbitrary. They are, in the end, so small and insignificant that one can only wonder why we put so much energy into achieving our life goals. This is the absurd condition we cannot escape.

It has been revealed that we must, therefore, acknowledge that the “absurdity of our situation derives not from a collision between our expectations and the world, but from a collision within ourselves.” I don’t agree with Nagel, in his claim to provide a superior account to that of Camus. If anything, Nagel reinforces Camus’ argument. For Camus as for Nagel, the search for final justifications in God, religion, power, family or the state is just as futile, for their purposes must appear just as absurd if we take a step back. They are no more than an escape from the absurd, not a solution. For now, it seems as if Camus’ notion of the absurd is compatible with contemporary analytical philosophy after all.

If you enjoyed this short essay, you might enjoy the much longer version, on which it is based, where I go into much more detail: click here.

Browning, H., & Veit, W. (2022). The Desperate Search for Meaning in Life. In C. Cotton & A. M. Winters (Eds.), Neon Genesis Evangelion and Philosophy (pp. 3–12). Chicago: Carus Books. [Download].

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that nesting season has officially begun for the seabirds visiting Midway Atoll National Wildlife Refuge near Hawaii.
  • In a recent development, black-footed albatrosses are typically the first to lay eggs beginning in November.
  • One special albatross couple has already been spotted—George and Geraldine.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that nesting season has officially begun for the seabirds visiting Midway Atoll National Wildlife Refuge near Hawaii. The first egg of the season was laid by a black-footed albatross (Phoebastria nigripes) or kaʻupu in Hawaiian. Field biologist and photographer Dan Rapp captured video of this exciting first, which Friends of Midway Atoll National Wildlife Refuge shared on social media.

In a recent development, black-footed albatrosses are typically the first to lay eggs beginning in November. The Laysan albatross (Phoebastria immutabilis) or mōlī in Hawaiian, will lay their eggs in late November through December. Every fall, this remote group of islands about 1,250 miles from Honolulu temporarily becomes the world’s largest albatross colony. Albatrosses are a group of large migratory seabird species, and includes the wandering albatross (Diomedea exulans), which has the largest wingspan of any living bird species.

One special albatross couple has already been spotted—George and Geraldine. The duo is together for the 10th straight year. George was first spotted exactly one month ago on October 18, and the couple was reunited by October 22. The pair are short-tailed albatrosses (Phoebastria albatrus) or makalena in Hawaiian. Short-tailed albatrosses can live up to 50 years and are monogamous—clearly.

Wisdom, a particularly famous bird in these parts, has not been spotted just yet. The over 70-year-old Laysan albatross is the oldest known banded wild bird in the world. She was first identified and banded in 1956 by wildlife biologist Chandler Robbins after she laid a single egg. Biologists estimate that she has produced 50 to 60 eggs and as many as 30 of her chicks have fledged in her lifetime. In 2024, Wisdom became the world’s oldest known wild bird to successfully lay an egg at the estimated age of 74. In March, she became a grandmother again.

Viewers can take in the sights and sounds of the albatross colony via live cameras and follow Friends of Midway Atoll National Wildlife Refuge for updates.

Viewers can expect to see the birds return to the islands, perform various courtship dances, begin to nest, lay their eggs, and eventually watch albatross chicks in all their fluffy glory.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that ford has entered the battery business.
  • In a recent development, how do you get more out of a battery without adding weight or more cells?
  • Industry observers note that unlike traditional lithium-ion, LFP batteries use no nickel or cobalt, which helps reduce costs.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that ford has entered the battery business. The first LFP battery cells are now rolling off the assembly line at Ford’s BlueOval Battery Park plant in Michigan and are headed to power Fathom prototypes in Kentucky.

In a recent development, how do you get more out of a battery without adding weight or more cells? According to Alan Clarke, Ford’s vice president of advanced development projects, who is also leading its Universal Electric Vehicle (UEV) platform, the answer lies in lithium iron phosphate (LFP) technology.

Industry observers note that unlike traditional lithium-ion, LFP batteries use no nickel or cobalt, which helps reduce costs. They also typically hold up better after years of use and charging.

To make it a reality, Ford turned to CATL, the leading global EV battery manufacturer. Ford uses CATL’s licensed technology and manufacturing expertise at its BlueOval Battery Park Michigan plant.

Ford said it will be the first in the US to deliver LFP batteries for mainstream automotive use, with the battery cells now rolling off the line in Michigan.

The first LFP battery cells are headed to Ford’s Louisville Assembly Plant and will be used to power Fathom prototypes, its first vehicle based on the UEV platform.

Recent findings suggest that ford designed and engineered the Fathom from the ground up for efficiency. As such, it chose prismatic battery cells because they fit directly into the chassis, reducing structural costs.

With cells now being delivered from a plant that it owns and operates, Ford remarked it will use the knowledge gained in Michigan to support more affordable EVs and Ford Energy, its new battery energy storage business in Kentucky.

At Ford’s new battery plant in Michigan, assembly lines can deliver 40 cells every minute, making it one of the fastest LFP prismatic battery assembly lines outside China.

Although the accelerated output drives down costs, Ford said employees use AI-powered image recognition and inspection tools to spot defects in real time and maintain quality.

“Our goal is to make defective cells so rare that we track their frequency per billion cells rather than per million,” Ford noted.

With production testing now underway, Ford aims to have the battery pack plant in Michigan up and running in 2027, ahead of schedule.

Ford will open preorders for the Fathom in early 2027, starting at $28,350 for the standard-range model.

CEO Jim Farley said on the firm’s third-quarter earnings call last month that the Fathom, Ford’s first vehicle based on the UEV platform, remains on track to launch in Q4 2027.

Farley noted the Fathom is a “breakthrough product” that’s highly capable and still affordable. The starting MSRP is under $30,000, and the low cost of ownership is perfect for today’s market, he added.

Sources indicate that ford and Slate both producing vehicles with US-produced LFP batteries is a great milestone. Hopefully we can keep pushing our domestic battery supply chain forward.

Ford said the Fathom will offer more interior space than a Toyota RAV4, and it will cost less to own over five years than a three-year-old used Tesla Model Y.

It has been revealed that the pickup will be the first vehicle to integrate Apple Maps directly into the navigation system. All versions will be BlueCruise-capable for hands-free driving, with standard Apple CarPlay and Android Auto, plus bidirectional charging capabilities.

Although we have yet to see it, Ford noted the Fathom features a “large touchscreen display” with easy-to-use navigation.

Ford has not revealed battery specs or range, but we do know the pickup will have an NACS port after several prototypes were spotted at a Tesla Supercharger over the summer.

💡 Key Takeaways
